Ecosystems.intro: An ecosystem includes all the living organisms and non-living factors in an area. Understanding how ecosystems work and how organisms interact is fundamental to B7.
Ecosystems.mnemonic: Remember the scale of ecological organisation with: 'Oh Pops, Can't Even Breathe' — Organism, Population, Community, Ecosystem, Biosphere. For abiotic vs biotic: 'Abiotic = All non-living things (temperature, light, pH); Biotic = Biological/living things (predators, competitors, disease)'.

sections.title: Key Ecological Terms
sections.text: Understanding these terms precisely is essential — AQA examiners test whether students can use them correctly.
points: Ecosystem — all living organisms (biotic) and non-living factors (abiotic) in an area, and their interactions
Population — all individuals of ONE species in a defined area at a given time
Community — all populations of DIFFERENT species living in an area
Habitat — the specific place within an ecosystem where an organism lives
Niche — the role an organism plays in its ecosystem, including what it eats and what eats it

sections.title: Abiotic and Biotic Factors
sections.text: Both abiotic (non-living) and biotic (living) factors affect the distribution and abundance of organisms.
points: Abiotic factors — light intensity, temperature, moisture level, soil pH, wind speed, CO₂ and O₂ concentration, salinity
Biotic factors — predation (reduces prey numbers), competition (reduces resources), disease, food availability, presence of pollinators

sections.title: Competition
sections.text: Competition occurs when organisms need the same limited resources.
points: Intraspecific competition — between individuals of the SAME species; most intense because they need identical resources
Interspecific competition — between individuals of DIFFERENT species; less intense if niches partially overlap
Resources competed for — food, water, space, light (plants), mates, nesting sites
Competitive exclusion — if two species compete for the same niche, one will eventually outcompete and replace the other

keyTerms.def: All living organisms and non-living factors in an area
Non-living factor affecting organisms (temperature, light, pH, etc.)
Living factor affecting organisms (predation, competition, disease)
All individuals of one species in an area
All populations of different species living together in an area
The place where an organism lives within an ecosystem
Competition between individuals of the same species
Competition between individuals of different species

examTips: Know the difference between population (one species), community (all species in area), and ecosystem (community PLUS all abiotic factors) — these are frequently tested in data questions.
Intraspecific competition is MORE intense than interspecific because members of the same species compete for IDENTICAL resources.
When asked how a change in an abiotic factor affects organisms, always explain the mechanism: e.g. less light → less photosynthesis → less food/biomass produced → fewer consumers can be supported.
commonMistakes: Confusing community (living organisms only — all species) with ecosystem (community PLUS all abiotic factors like temperature and pH).
Forgetting to give examples of abiotic factors — temperature, light, pH, and moisture are all commonly tested.
Saying predation is an abiotic factor — predation is a BIOTIC factor because predators are living organisms.
clozePassages: An ecosystem includes all the living organisms (biotic factors) and non-living components (abiotic factors) in an area, and their interactions. Biotic factors include predators, prey, and competitors. Abiotic factors include temperature, light intensity, pH, and availability of water and minerals. Changes in either type of factor can have significant effects on all organisms in the ecosystem.

Producers are organisms that make their own food by photosynthesis — usually plants. Primary consumers eat producers. Secondary consumers eat primary consumers. Tertiary consumers eat secondary consumers. Energy is lost at each stage, which is why food chains rarely have more than five trophic levels. Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi break down dead organisms, returning nutrients to the soil.

Organisms in an ecosystem are interdependent — changes to one population affect others. Competition occurs between organisms for the same resources. Interspecific competition occurs between different species. Intraspecific competition occurs within the same species. Predator-prey relationships show cyclical patterns — as prey numbers increase, predator numbers increase, which then causes prey numbers to fall again.

Food Webs.intro: Food chains and food webs show feeding relationships between organisms. Energy flows through ecosystems from producers to consumers.
Food Webs.mnemonic: Remember: 'Arrows show where the Energy goes' — not who eats who in terms of direction, but the direction of energy transfer (from eaten to eater). For energy loss, think of the '10% rule': only 10% of energy at each trophic level makes it to the next — the other 90% is lost as heat (respiration), movement, and undigested waste.

sections.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
sections.text: Food chains show single feeding pathways; food webs show all the interconnected feeding relationships in an ecosystem.
points: Food chain — shows ONE pathway: producer → primary consumer → secondary consumer → tertiary consumer
Food web — shows MULTIPLE interconnected food chains; more realistic model of an ecosystem
Arrow direction — arrows show the direction of ENERGY TRANSFER (from the organism being eaten to the one eating it)
Always starts with a producer — all food chains begin with a plant or other photosynthetic organism

sections.title: Energy Transfer Between Trophic Levels
sections.text: Energy is lost at each trophic level, which limits the length of food chains and the size of populations at higher levels.
points: Approximately 10% of energy transfers between trophic levels
Lost as heat — energy used in respiration is released as heat, which cannot be reused
Lost as undigested material — some food passes through as faeces and is not absorbed
Lost as movement — energy used for locomotion is converted to heat
Short food chains — because so much energy is lost, food chains rarely exceed 4–5 trophic levels

sections.title: Pyramids of Biomass and Numbers
sections.text: Pyramids represent the amount of biomass or number of organisms at each trophic level.
points: Pyramid of biomass — always a true pyramid shape (wider at base); shows the total dry mass at each level
Pyramid of numbers — can be unusual shapes (e.g. one tree supporting thousands of caterpillars gives an inverted base)
Biomass decreases at each level — because energy is lost at each transfer

callout.label: Pyramids
callout.text: Pyramid of biomass — always a true pyramid (wider at base). Pyramid of numbers can be unusual shape (e.g. many insects on one tree).

keyTerms.def: An organism that makes its own food by photosynthesis (plants, algae)
An organism that eats other organisms for energy
The position of an organism in a food chain
The total mass of living material at a trophic level
A diagram showing the relative mass of organisms at each trophic level — always pyramid-shaped
The build-up of toxic substances at higher trophic levels as predators consume many prey

examTips: Arrows in food chains and food webs show the direction of ENERGY FLOW — not 'is eaten by'. A common error is drawing arrows backwards.
Only approximately 10% of energy passes between trophic levels — explain what happens to the other 90%: lost as heat through respiration, movement, and undigested material in faeces.
Pyramid of biomass is ALWAYS a true pyramid shape — but pyramid of numbers can be inverted if a large organism (e.g. a tree) supports many small ones.
commonMistakes: Drawing food chain arrows from consumer to producer — the arrow always points in the direction of energy flow: from the organism eaten TO the organism eating.
Saying ALL pyramids of numbers are pyramid-shaped — they are NOT always pyramidal (e.g. one oak tree → thousands of caterpillars → hundreds of birds).
Forgetting the three ways energy is lost between trophic levels — heat from respiration, undigested material (faeces), and energy used for movement.
clozePassages: A food web shows the feeding relationships between many organisms in an ecosystem. Each organism can be part of several food chains. Removing or reducing one species from a food web can have knock-on effects throughout the ecosystem. Producers form the base of all food webs. The arrows in a food web show the direction of energy transfer — from the organism being eaten to the one eating it.

Energy is transferred along food chains but is lost at each trophic level. Energy is lost through heat from respiration, movement, and undigested material in faeces. Only about 10% of energy is transferred from one level to the next. This means that biomass decreases at each trophic level. This is represented in a pyramid of biomass, which always has a wider base and narrows towards the top.

Bioaccumulation occurs when toxic substances become more concentrated at higher trophic levels in a food chain. For example, DDT (a pesticide) accumulates in the fatty tissues of organisms. At each level, the predator consumes many prey organisms, so the concentration of the toxin increases. Top predators can accumulate dangerously high concentrations. This caused serious declines in bird of prey populations before DDT was banned.

Nutrient Cycling.intro: Nutrients are constantly recycled through ecosystems. The carbon and water cycles are the main examples you need for GCSE Combined Science.
Nutrient Cycling.mnemonic: For the carbon cycle, think of carbon's journey: 'Plants Catch Carbon (photosynthesis); All Living Things Release it (respiration); Dead Things Decay and Release it (decomposition); Burning Releases Old Carbon (combustion of fossil fuels).' For the water cycle: 'Evaporation → Condensation → Precipitation → Runoff → Evaporation again' — a never-ending circle, like a shower you can't turn off.

sections.title: The Carbon Cycle
sections.text: Carbon moves continuously between living organisms, the atmosphere, and the Earth through a series of processes.
points: Photosynthesis — removes CO₂ from atmosphere; plants convert carbon into organic molecules (carbon fixation)
Respiration — releases CO₂ back to atmosphere; all living organisms respire
Decomposition — decomposers break down dead organisms; CO₂ released by respiration
Combustion — burning fossil fuels and wood releases CO₂ that was stored for millions of years
Feeding — carbon passes along food chains when consumers eat producers

sections.title: The Water Cycle
sections.text: Water moves continuously through the environment through a cycle driven by solar energy and gravity.
points: Evaporation — water from oceans, lakes, and land surface heated by Sun becomes water vapour
Transpiration — water vapour released from plant leaves through stomata
Condensation — water vapour cools at altitude, condenses into water droplets forming clouds
Precipitation — rain, snow or hail falls from clouds back to land and sea
Runoff and infiltration — water flows into rivers and lakes or soaks into groundwater

sections.title: Decomposers in Nutrient Cycling
sections.text: Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) are essential for returning nutrients locked in dead organisms back to the ecosystem.
points: Break down dead matter — decomposers secrete enzymes to digest dead organisms and animal waste externally
Release mineral ions — nitrates, phosphates, and other ions returned to soil; available for plant uptake
Release CO₂ — through aerobic respiration during decomposition
Without decomposers — nutrients would become permanently locked in dead organic matter and ecosystems would collapse

keyTerms.def: The cycling of carbon through living organisms, the atmosphere and the Earth
Organism (bacteria/fungi) that breaks down dead material, recycling nutrients
Burning — releases stored carbon as CO₂
Process by which plants remove CO₂ from the atmosphere and fix carbon into organic molecules
Loss of water vapour from plant leaves — contributes to the water cycle
Rain, snow, or hail — returns water from the atmosphere to land

examTips: Decomposers release CO₂ through RESPIRATION — they do not photosynthesize. This is a common confusion.
Photosynthesis removes CO₂ from the atmosphere; respiration, decomposition, and combustion all add CO₂ back.
For a 6-mark question on the carbon cycle, name all four processes: photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, and combustion — and state whether each adds or removes CO₂.
commonMistakes: Saying decomposers photosynthesise — they are heterotrophs that respire; they release CO₂ through aerobic respiration.
Forgetting combustion as a major way CO₂ enters the atmosphere — burning fossil fuels releases carbon that has been locked up for millions of years.
Confusing the water cycle and carbon cycle — water cycles through evaporation, condensation, precipitation; carbon cycles through photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, combustion.
clozePassages: The carbon cycle describes how carbon moves through living organisms and the environment. Carbon dioxide is removed from the atmosphere by photosynthesis. It is returned by respiration, combustion, and decomposition. Carbon is stored in organisms, fossil fuels, and the oceans. Human activities such as burning fossil fuels are increasing CO₂ levels in the atmosphere, contributing to climate change.

The nitrogen cycle describes how nitrogen moves through ecosystems. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in soil and root nodules convert atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia. Nitrifying bacteria convert ammonia to nitrates. Plants absorb nitrates through roots to make proteins. Animals obtain nitrogen by eating plants or other animals. Denitrifying bacteria convert nitrates back to atmospheric nitrogen, completing the cycle.

Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi break down dead organisms and waste materials. They release enzymes that digest organic matter into simple inorganic molecules including nitrates, phosphates, and carbon dioxide. These molecules are returned to the soil and atmosphere, making them available for plants again. Without decomposers, nutrients would become locked in dead matter and ecosystems would fail.

Decomposition.intro: Decomposition is the breakdown of dead organic matter by decomposers. It is essential for recycling nutrients back into ecosystems.
Decomposition.mnemonic: Remember factors affecting decomposition rate with 'TOMOP': Temperature (higher = faster up to optimum); Oxygen (more aerobic = faster); Moisture (wetter = faster); Organism type (bacteria and fungi are the key decomposers); pH (neutral optimal). Think of a compost heap — warm, turned (adds oxygen), moist = fast breakdown.

sections.title: Decomposers
sections.text: Bacteria and fungi are the main decomposers — they break down dead matter by secreting digestive enzymes.
points: Bacteria and fungi — the two groups of organisms that act as decomposers
Extracellular digestion — decomposers secrete enzymes OUTSIDE their cells to digest dead matter, then absorb the products
Break down dead plants and animals — and animal waste products like faeces
Release mineral ions — nitrates, phosphates, and other ions into the soil for plant uptake
Release CO₂ — through aerobic respiration; and methane in anaerobic conditions

sections.title: Factors Affecting Decomposition Rate
sections.text: The rate of decomposition depends on environmental conditions that affect the activity of decomposing microorganisms.
points: Temperature — higher temperature increases enzyme activity and decomposition rate (up to optimum ~40°C; above this, enzymes denature and rate falls)
Moisture/water availability — decomposers need water for chemical reactions; more moisture = faster decomposition
Oxygen availability — aerobic decomposition is much faster than anaerobic; turning compost adds oxygen
pH — neutral pH is generally optimal; very acidic or alkaline conditions slow enzyme activity

sections.title: Practical Applications
sections.text: Understanding decomposition has important practical applications in waste management and energy production.
points: Composting — controlled aerobic decomposition of organic waste; turning the heap adds oxygen and speeds the process; produces nutrient-rich compost for soil
Sewage treatment — decomposers break down organic waste in sewage; treated water is cleaner and safer
Biogas generators — sealed tanks allow anaerobic decomposition of animal waste; produces methane gas used as a renewable fuel
Food preservation — refrigeration, freezing, drying, and pickling slow decomposition by removing ideal conditions

keyTerms.def: The breakdown of dead organic matter by bacteria and fungi
Organism that breaks down dead organic material (bacteria and fungi)
Controlled aerobic decomposition of organic waste to produce compost
Decomposition in the presence of oxygen — faster than anaerobic
Decomposition without oxygen — slower; produces methane
Methane produced by anaerobic decomposition, used as a fuel

examTips: Decomposition is faster in warm, moist, aerobic conditions — state all three when asked what conditions speed up decomposition.
Decomposers are bacteria AND fungi — both groups are involved; do not say just bacteria.
Composting works better when turned regularly — turning introduces oxygen, shifting from anaerobic (slow) to aerobic (faster) decomposition.
commonMistakes: Forgetting that decomposers are bacteria AND fungi — not just bacteria; fungi (e.g. moulds) are equally important decomposers.
Saying decomposition always needs oxygen — anaerobic decomposition DOES occur (in waterlogged soils, sealed biogas tanks) but is slower than aerobic decomposition.
Saying high temperatures always speed up decomposition — above the enzyme's optimum temperature (~40°C for most decomposers), enzymes denature and decomposition slows or stops.
clozePassages: Decomposition is the breakdown of dead organisms and waste by microorganisms such as bacteria and fungi. The rate of decomposition is affected by temperature, moisture, and oxygen levels. Warm, moist, and aerobic conditions favour rapid decomposition. In cold, dry, or waterlogged conditions, decomposition is slow. This is why organisms preserved in ice or peat bogs can remain intact for thousands of years.

Compost is produced by decomposing organic waste. Garden compost heaps decompose plant material such as leaves and vegetable peelings using bacteria and fungi. Turning the compost heap introduces oxygen, speeding up aerobic decomposition. Adding materials with both high carbon and nitrogen content provides a good balance for decomposers. Finished compost improves soil structure and provides nutrients for plants.

In the absence of oxygen, anaerobic decomposition takes place. This produces methane (biogas) and is slower than aerobic decomposition. Biogas generators use anaerobic decomposition of animal waste and plant material to produce methane, which can be burned as a fuel. Anaerobic conditions in waterlogged soils can lead to the production of methane, which is a significant greenhouse gas contributing to climate change.

Biodiversity.intro: Biodiversity is the variety of living organisms in an ecosystem. High biodiversity is important for ecosystem stability and resilience.
Biodiversity.mnemonic: Biodiversity = variety in THREE senses: 'GSE — Genetic diversity within species; Species diversity (number of different species); Ecosystem diversity (variety of habitats)'. To remember why biodiversity matters, think 'FMESI': Food security, Medicines, Ecosystem services, Stability, Intrinsic value of all life.

sections.title: What is Biodiversity?
sections.text: Biodiversity encompasses the variety of life at all levels — from genetic variation within populations to the variety of ecosystems.
points: Species diversity — the variety of different species in an area; measured by species richness and evenness
Genetic diversity — the variety of alleles within a species; important for a species' ability to adapt
Ecosystem diversity — the variety of different habitats and ecosystems in a region
High biodiversity — makes ecosystems more stable; if one species is lost, others can fill the ecological role
Decline — human activities have significantly reduced global biodiversity

sections.title: Why Biodiversity Matters
sections.text: Biodiversity provides direct and indirect benefits to humans and is essential for the functioning of life on Earth.
points: Food security — wild plants are genetic reservoirs for developing new, disease-resistant crop varieties
Medicines — many important drugs are derived from wild plants and animals (e.g. aspirin from willow bark, penicillin from fungi)
Ecosystem services — clean water filtration, air purification, pollination of crops, climate regulation
Stability — biodiverse ecosystems are more resilient to change and recover better from disturbance
Intrinsic value — many argue all species have a right to exist, regardless of their direct value to humans

sections.title: Measuring Biodiversity
sections.text: Biodiversity is measured using both species richness (number of species) and species evenness (distribution of individuals).
points: Species richness — total number of different species present; higher is better
Species evenness — how equally the individuals are distributed among species; a habitat dominated by one species has low evenness
Indicator species — species whose presence or absence indicates environmental quality (e.g. lichens = clean air; rat-tailed maggots = polluted water)

callout.label: Species Richness vs Evenness
callout.text: Biodiversity considers both the NUMBER of different species AND how evenly distributed they are. High numbers of only one species does not mean high biodiversity.

keyTerms.def: The variety of different species in an ecosystem
The number of different species in an area
Benefits that humans receive from functioning ecosystems
The variety of alleles within a population of a species
Species whose presence or abundance indicates the quality of the environment
How equally individuals are distributed among species in an area

examTips: High biodiversity leads to a more STABLE ecosystem — if one species declines, others can partially fill its role.
Biodiversity has been declining due to human activities — deforestation, pollution, overhunting, and climate change are the main causes.
Be able to suggest and evaluate methods of preserving biodiversity — conservation programmes, breeding programmes, seed banks, protected areas.
commonMistakes: Thinking biodiversity just means a large number of ONE species — it requires VARIETY of species (species richness) AND even distribution (species evenness).
Forgetting that genetic diversity WITHIN species is part of biodiversity — a species with very low genetic diversity is vulnerable to extinction.
Saying 'more plants = more biodiversity' — plants are just one type of organism; true biodiversity considers all species, including insects, fungi, bacteria, etc.
clozePassages: Biodiversity refers to the variety of all life on Earth — the number of different species, the genetic variation within species, and the variety of ecosystems. High biodiversity makes ecosystems more stable and resilient to change. Loss of biodiversity reduces ecosystem stability. The main threats to biodiversity include habitat destruction, pollution, climate change, invasive species, and overexploitation.

Maintaining biodiversity is important for several reasons. Ecosystems provide ecosystem services such as clean air and water, pollination, and climate regulation. Many medicines are derived from wild species. Future crops may need wild genetic diversity to withstand new diseases. Methods to protect biodiversity include conservation programmes, breeding programmes in zoos, seed banks, and international agreements such as the Convention on Biological Diversity.

Indicator species are organisms whose presence, absence, or abundance reflects the condition of the environment. Lichens are sensitive to air pollution and their presence indicates clean air. Freshwater invertebrates such as stonefly larvae indicate clean water. Rat-tailed maggots indicate polluted water. Monitoring indicator species provides a cost-effective way to assess environmental quality without expensive chemical analysis.

Climate Change.intro: Human activities are increasing greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere, causing global warming and climate change with major ecological consequences.
Climate Change.mnemonic: Greenhouse gases trap heat — remember 'CM W' (Carbon dioxide, Methane, Water vapour) are the three main greenhouse gases. For human causes of increased CO₂, use 'FDAL': Fossil fuels burned; Deforestation (less photosynthesis); Agriculture (cattle methane); Landfill (anaerobic methane). The natural greenhouse effect is essential for life — it's the ENHANCED version that causes problems.

sections.title: The Greenhouse Effect
sections.text: The greenhouse effect is a natural process essential for life on Earth — but human activities are enhancing it.
points: Short-wave radiation — from the Sun passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth's surface
Re-emitted as infrared — the warmed Earth radiates longer-wave (infrared) radiation upwards
Greenhouse gases absorb infrared — CO₂, methane, and water vapour trap this heat in the atmosphere
Natural greenhouse effect — essential for maintaining temperatures that support life; without it, Earth would be ~33°C colder
Enhanced greenhouse effect — increased greenhouse gases trap MORE heat, causing global temperatures to rise

sections.title: Human Causes of Climate Change
sections.text: Human activities since industrialisation have dramatically increased concentrations of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere.
points: Burning fossil fuels — releases CO₂ from coal, oil, and gas (electricity generation, transport, heating)
Deforestation — fewer trees means less photosynthesis to absorb CO₂; burning or rotting trees releases stored carbon
Agriculture — cattle produce methane through digestion; rice paddies produce methane during anaerobic decomposition
Landfill — anaerobic decomposition of buried waste produces methane

sections.title: Ecological Consequences
sections.text: Climate change is already affecting ecosystems worldwide, with accelerating impacts predicted for the future.
points: Rising sea levels — thermal expansion of ocean water and melting polar ice floods coastal habitats
Species distribution shifts — species move towards poles and to higher altitudes as temperatures increase
Ecosystem disruption — changing seasons alter migration patterns, flowering times, and food availability
Extinction risk — species unable to adapt or migrate fast enough face extinction
Extreme weather — increased frequency and intensity of floods, droughts, heatwaves, and storms

keyTerms.def: Trapping of heat in the atmosphere by greenhouse gases
Rise in average global temperature due to enhanced greenhouse effect
Total amount of greenhouse gases produced by human activities
Gas that absorbs infrared radiation and traps heat in the atmosphere (CO₂, methane, water vapour)
Large-scale removal of forests, releasing stored carbon and reducing photosynthesis
The increased trapping of heat due to human-increased greenhouse gas concentrations

examTips: Be able to evaluate evidence for climate change — scientists use data from ice cores, sea level records, temperature measurements, and species distribution data.
Methane is a much more potent greenhouse gas than CO₂ — from livestock, landfill, rice paddies, and permafrost thaw.
Climate change affects biodiversity — as habitats change, species that cannot adapt or migrate quickly enough may go extinct.
commonMistakes: Confusing the greenhouse effect (the natural process that warms the Earth) with global warming (the enhanced version causing climate change due to human activities).

Saying the ozone hole causes climate change — the ozone hole (over Antarctica, caused by CFCs) and climate change are SEPARATE issues. The ozone hole affects UV radiation; climate change is about heat trapping.
Thinking deforestation only matters because it releases CO₂ — it also matters because fewer trees means LESS CO₂ absorbed by photosynthesis.
clozePassages: Climate change is the long-term shift in global temperatures and weather patterns. It is driven by increased levels of greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane in the atmosphere. These gases trap heat from the sun, causing the greenhouse effect. Human activities — particularly burning fossil fuels and deforestation — have significantly increased CO₂ levels. Global temperatures have risen by approximately 1°C since pre-industrial times.

The effects of climate change include rising sea levels due to melting polar ice and thermal expansion of oceans. Extreme weather events such as hurricanes, droughts, and floods are becoming more frequent and intense. Many species face extinction as their habitats change faster than they can adapt. Changes in the distribution of species are already being observed. Coral reefs are being damaged by ocean acidification caused by increased CO₂ dissolving in seawater.

Deforestation contributes to climate change in two ways. Fewer trees means less photosynthesis, so less CO₂ is removed from the atmosphere. When trees are burned or decompose, the carbon stored in them is released as CO₂. Deforestation also reduces biodiversity and disrupts water cycles. Planting trees (afforestation) can help absorb CO₂ and is one strategy to mitigate climate change.

Maintaining Biodiversity.intro: Maintaining biodiversity requires active conservation efforts at local, national, and international levels. A range of strategies can protect endangered species and habitats.
Maintaining Biodiversity.mnemonic: Remember conservation methods with 'BREATHE': Breeding programmes (zoos/captive); Reforestation; Education and awareness; Agreements (international treaties); Terrestrial and marine protected areas; Habitat corridors; Ex-situ vs in-situ conservation. In-situ = 'In the Situation' (protecting habitat in the wild). Ex-situ = 'Exiting the situation' (protecting outside natural habitat — zoos, seed banks).

sections.title: In-Situ Conservation
sections.text: In-situ conservation protects species in their natural habitat — generally considered more effective than ex-situ methods.
points: Nature reserves and national parks — areas where human activity is restricted to protect habitats and species
Marine conservation zones — protected sea areas where fishing and development are restricted
Habitat restoration — replanting vegetation, removing invasive species, and restoring degraded habitats
Reforestation — planting new forests to replace those lost to deforestation
Advantages — species remain in their natural environment; full ecosystem preserved; self-sustaining populations

sections.title: Ex-Situ Conservation
sections.text: Ex-situ conservation protects species outside their natural habitat — an important safety net for critically endangered species.
points: Zoo captive breeding programmes — endangered species bred in captivity with the aim of reintroduction to the wild
Seed banks — frozen seeds of plant species stored as insurance against extinction (e.g. Svalbard Global Seed Vault)
Botanical gardens — cultivate and preserve rare plant species
Gene banks — store genetic material (DNA, gametes, embryos) from endangered species
Limitations — animals may struggle to survive when reintroduced; expensive; does not address habitat destruction

sections.title: International Agreements and Sustainable Practices
sections.text: Protecting biodiversity requires global cooperation because species and their habitats cross national borders.
points: CITES — Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species; bans trade in endangered species
Paris Agreement — international commitment to limit global warming, which threatens biodiversity
Sustainable fishing — fishing quotas and size limits prevent populations falling below sustainable levels
Sustainable agriculture — reducing pesticide use, maintaining hedgerows, crop rotation to support biodiversity
Education — raising awareness of biodiversity loss encourages behaviour change and political pressure

keyTerms.def: Protecting species within their natural habitat
Protecting species outside their natural habitat (zoos, seed banks)
Breeding endangered animals in captivity with the aim of reintroduction
A facility that stores frozen seeds of plant species as a safeguard against extinction
A protected area where human activity is limited to conserve habitats and species
Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species — bans trade in threatened species

examTips: In-situ conservation (protecting habitat in the wild) is generally better than ex-situ (zoo/seed bank) because species remain in their natural ecosystem.
Captive breeding programmes are only effective if the wild habitat is also protected — releasing animals into a destroyed habitat will not save the species.
For evaluate questions on conservation, always give both advantages and disadvantages of each method before reaching a conclusion.
commonMistakes: Saying zoos alone can save species — captive breeding must be combined with habitat protection (in-situ conservation) for long-term success.
Forgetting that seed banks store plant genetic diversity — they are not just for food crops; they preserve wild plant species too.
Thinking conservation is just about protecting charismatic animals — protecting entire ecosystems (habitats, insects, fungi, plants) is what ultimately maintains biodiversity.
clozePassages: In-situ conservation involves protecting species in their natural habitat. Examples include nature reserves, national parks, and marine conservation zones. Habitat restoration projects remove invasive species and replant native vegetation. In-situ conservation is generally preferred because it preserves the full ecosystem and allows species to maintain natural behaviours. However, it requires large areas of land and cooperation from local communities.

Ex-situ conservation protects species outside their natural habitat. Captive breeding programmes in zoos aim to maintain populations of endangered species and eventually reintroduce them to the wild. Seed banks such as the Svalbard Global Seed Vault store seeds from thousands of plant species at very low temperatures. Ex-situ conservation acts as a safety net but cannot replace the need to protect wild habitats.

Maintaining biodiversity requires international cooperation. CITES bans trade in endangered species. The Convention on Biological Diversity commits countries to protecting their natural heritage. Sustainable fishing quotas prevent fish stocks from collapsing. Education and awareness campaigns encourage behaviour change. Reducing carbon emissions is crucial to slow climate change, which is one of the greatest long-term threats to global biodiversity.

Trophic Levels.intro: Trophic levels describe the feeding position of an organism in an ecosystem. Energy is transferred but significantly lost between each trophic level, limiting the length of food chains.
Trophic Levels.mnemonic: Remember the trophic levels with: 'Pretty Penguins Can't Eat Dead Things' — Producers, Primary consumers, Secondary consumers, Tertiary consumers, (and then Decomposers at the end). For energy efficiency at 10%, imagine starting with 1000 kJ in plants: only 100 kJ reaches herbivores, 10 kJ reaches carnivores, and just 1 kJ reaches top predators.

sections.title: What Are Trophic Levels?
sections.text: Trophic levels number the feeding position of an organism in a food chain, starting at 1 for producers.
points: Trophic level 1 — Producers: plants, algae, and other photosynthetic organisms that fix energy from sunlight
Trophic level 2 — Primary consumers: herbivores that eat producers (e.g. rabbits, caterpillars, zooplankton)
Trophic level 3 — Secondary consumers: carnivores that eat primary consumers (e.g. foxes, small fish)
Trophic level 4 — Tertiary consumers: carnivores that eat secondary consumers (e.g. eagles, sharks)
Decomposers: feed on dead organisms from any trophic level; recycle nutrients back to producers

sections.title: Energy Transfer Between Trophic Levels
sections.text: Only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next level — the rest is lost.
points: 10% rule — approximately 10% of energy transfers to the next trophic level
Lost as heat — the majority of energy is used in respiration and released as heat to the environment
Lost as undigested material — some food passes through as faeces without being fully digested
Lost through movement — energy used for locomotion and maintaining body temperature is released as heat
Consequence — biomass and population size decrease at each successive trophic level

sections.title: Efficiency and Food Production
sections.text: Understanding trophic levels has important implications for food production and global food security.
points: Shorter food chains are more efficient — eating plants (trophic level 2) delivers far more energy per hectare than eating meat (trophic level 3 or 4)
Land use — producing 1 kg of beef requires far more land and energy than producing 1 kg of wheat
Global food security — as the human population grows, shifting diets towards plant-based foods could help feed more people using the same amount of land
Factory farming — reduces energy losses by limiting animal movement and controlling temperature, but raises ethical concerns

keyTerms.def: The feeding position of an organism in a food chain (1 = producer, 2 = primary consumer, etc.)
Trophic level 1 — organisms that make their own food by photosynthesis
Trophic level 2 — herbivores that eat producers
Trophic level 3 — carnivores that eat primary consumers
Trophic level 4 — carnivores that eat secondary consumers
The percentage of energy at one trophic level transferred to the next (approximately 10%)

examTips: Only approximately 10% of energy transfers between each trophic level — in a calculation, multiply by 0.1 (or divide by 10) for each step up the food chain.
Always explain WHERE the energy goes when it is 'lost': heat from respiration, undigested material in faeces, and energy used for movement.
Eating lower in the food chain (closer to producers) is more energy-efficient — this is relevant to sustainable food production questions.
commonMistakes: Saying energy is 'destroyed' at each trophic level — energy is not destroyed; it is converted to heat and lost to the environment. Energy is CONSERVED but becomes unavailable for the next trophic level.
Forgetting decomposers — they are not usually shown in pyramids but they feed on ALL trophic levels and are essential for nutrient recycling.
Confusing biomass pyramid (always true pyramid shape) with pyramid of numbers (can be inverted — e.g. one tree can support thousands of insects).
clozePassages: A trophic level describes the feeding position of an organism in a food chain. Producers occupy trophic level 1 and make their own food through photosynthesis. Primary consumers (herbivores) are at trophic level 2. Secondary consumers eat primary consumers at trophic level 3. Energy is transferred between levels, but most is lost as heat from respiration, limiting food chains to around 4–5 levels.

Only approximately 10% of the energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next. The remaining 90% is lost as heat through respiration, through undigested material in faeces, and through energy used in movement. This means that populations and biomass decrease at each trophic level. This is represented by a pyramid of biomass, which always has a wider base and narrows towards the top.

Understanding trophic levels has implications for food security. Eating plant foods (trophic level 2) is far more energy-efficient than eating meat (trophic level 3 or 4) because fewer energy transfers mean less energy is lost. As the global population grows, producing more food from fewer resources will be essential. Reducing meat consumption and growing more plant crops could help ensure enough food for everyone using the available agricultural land.

Human Impact on Ecosystems.intro: Human activities have dramatically altered ecosystems worldwide. Understanding these impacts and ways to reduce them is important for B7.
Human Impact on Ecosystems.mnemonic: Remember human impacts with 'DOPPLE': Deforestation; Over-fishing; Pollution (water, air, plastic); Pesticides and fertilisers; Land use change (urbanisation, peat drainage); Extinction through habitat loss. For eutrophication, remember the chain: 'Fertiliser → Algal bloom → Light blocked → Plants die → Bacteria decompose → Oxygen depleted → Fish die'.

sections.title: Deforestation
sections.text: Large-scale removal of forests has major consequences for biodiversity, the carbon cycle, and climate.
points: Reasons for deforestation — clearing land for agriculture (especially cattle ranching and palm oil), timber extraction, urban development
Biodiversity loss — tropical rainforests contain over half the world's species; deforestation causes mass extinction
Carbon release — burning or decomposing trees releases stored carbon as CO₂; contributes to climate change
Less photosynthesis — fewer trees means less CO₂ absorbed from atmosphere
Soil erosion — tree roots hold soil; without them, topsoil washes away, reducing fertility

sections.title: Land Use Changes and Pollution
sections.text: Urbanisation, farming practices, and pollution all damage ecosystems and reduce biodiversity.
points: Urbanisation — building on natural land destroys habitats and fragments ecosystems
Monoculture farming — growing a single crop species reduces biodiversity and removes hedgerows that support wildlife
Peat bog drainage — releases stored CO₂; destroys important wetland habitat for rare species
Eutrophication — fertiliser runoff → excess nitrates in water → algal blooms → plants die → bacteria decompose → oxygen depleted → fish die
Plastic pollution — marine animals ingest or become entangled; persists for centuries in the environment

sections.title: Conservation Methods
sections.text: A range of conservation strategies can help protect and restore ecosystems damaged by human activity.
points: Protected areas — national parks, nature reserves, and marine conservation zones restrict damaging activities
Captive breeding programmes — breed endangered species in zoos for eventual reintroduction to wild
Reforestation — replanting native trees restores habitat and increases carbon sequestration
Sustainable fishing — quotas and size limits prevent overfishing; Marine Stewardship Council certification
Reducing emissions — switching to renewable energy reduces CO₂ and methane contributions to climate change

sections.title: Pollution Consequences
sections.text: Different types of pollution have specific damaging effects on ecosystems.
points: Air pollution — acid rain damages trees and changes soil pH; smog reduces photosynthesis
Water pollution — eutrophication from fertilisers; heavy metals from industry are toxic to aquatic life
Pesticide bioaccumulation — toxins concentrate at higher trophic levels; top predators worst affected
Plastic pollution — seabirds and marine mammals die from ingestion or entanglement; microplastics enter food chains

keyTerms.def: Clearing large areas of forest, often for agriculture or development
Excess nutrients in water causing algal blooms and death of aquatic organisms
Build-up of toxins in organisms at higher trophic levels
Protection and management of natural environments and biodiversity
Growing a single crop species over a large area — reduces biodiversity
Rain made acidic by dissolved sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from combustion

examTips: Eutrophication is a CHAIN of events — state all steps: fertiliser runoff → algal bloom → blocks light → underwater plants die → decomposing bacteria use up oxygen → fish and other aquatic organisms die.
Bioaccumulation: toxins concentrate at higher trophic levels because predators eat many prey — top predators accumulate the most.
Be able to evaluate conservation methods — give costs, benefits, and practicality for each one.
commonMistakes: Confusing the stages of eutrophication — it's a cascade of events, not just 'fertiliser kills fish'. The algal bloom is just the first step.
Forgetting that peat bogs are important carbon stores — draining them releases CO₂ stored over thousands of years.
Saying only factories cause pollution — agricultural fertiliser runoff (eutrophication), pesticides, and livestock methane are all major pollutants from farming.
clozePassages: Human activities have caused significant damage to ecosystems. Deforestation destroys habitats and reduces biodiversity. Agricultural practices including the use of pesticides and fertilisers can harm wildlife and cause water pollution. Urbanisation destroys habitats. Overfishing reduces fish populations below sustainable levels. These pressures have caused many species to become threatened or extinct.

Eutrophication occurs when excess nitrates and phosphates from fertilisers enter waterways. This causes rapid growth of algae called an algal bloom, which blocks light from underwater plants, causing them to die. Decomposers break down the dead plants, using up oxygen in the process. This causes other aquatic organisms to die due to oxygen depletion. Eutrophication is a serious problem in many rivers and lakes.

Pollution from human activities takes many forms. Air pollution from vehicle exhausts and industry causes acid rain and smog, damaging ecosystems. Water pollution from sewage, pesticides, and industrial waste harms aquatic organisms. Plastic pollution in oceans harms marine life through entanglement and ingestion. Reducing pollution requires international cooperation, legislation, and changes in industrial processes and individual behaviour.

Sampling.intro: Scientists use sampling techniques to estimate the size of populations and measure biodiversity without counting every individual.
Sampling.mnemonic: Remember the three main sampling methods: 'QTM — Quadrats for plants (stationary); Transects for gradients (change across habitat); Mark-release-recapture for Mobile animals'. For mark-release-recapture formula, remember: 'First catch × Second catch ÷ Marked recaught' = population estimate. Or think: 'If you marked 10 out of 100, and get 10% back, the population must be 100'.

sections.title: Quadrats
sections.text: Quadrats are square frames used to sample stationary or slow-moving organisms in a habitat.
points: Use — for stationary organisms (plants) or slow-moving animals; count number of each species within the frame
Placement must be RANDOM — use random number coordinates from a grid to avoid bias
Calculate population estimate — (mean count per quadrat ÷ quadrat area) × total habitat area
Sample size — more quadrats = more reliable estimate; reduces effect of unusual local patches
% cover — for plants, estimate the percentage of each species covering the quadrat area

sections.title: Transects
sections.text: Transects record how species distribution changes across a habitat along a line.
points: Line transect — record every organism touching a tape measure stretched across the habitat
Belt transect — quadrats placed at regular intervals along the transect line; records species on either side
Use — studying how organisms change along an environmental gradient (e.g. from sea shore to inland, or from shaded woodland edge to open field)
Systematic sampling — not random; positioned deliberately to capture environmental gradients

sections.title: Mark-Release-Recapture
sections.text: Mark-release-recapture (capture-recapture) estimates the size of mobile animal populations.
numbered: Capture a sample, count and mark them (e.g. paint spot on wing)
Release and allow marked individuals to mix fully with the population
After sufficient time, capture a second sample
Count total in second sample and count how many are marked
Calculate population estimate using the Lincoln Index formula
points: Lincoln Index formula — Population = (first catch × second catch) ÷ number of marked in second catch
Assumptions — marks are not lost or harmful; population is closed (no immigration, emigration, births, or deaths between catches); marked individuals mix randomly

callout.label: Lincoln Index Formula
callout.text: Population estimate = (first catch × second catch) ÷ number of marked individuals in second catch. Assumptions: marks not lost/harmful, population closed (no births/deaths/migration).

keyTerms.def: A square frame used to sample stationary organisms in an area
A line through a habitat used to study distribution of organisms
Technique used to estimate the size of animal populations
Sampling with no pattern or bias — using random coordinates
Formula for population estimate: (n1 × n2) ÷ m2
Quadrats placed at regular intervals along a transect line to study species distribution

examTips: Quadrats MUST be placed randomly using random number coordinates — placing them by eye or in convenient spots introduces bias.
Mark-release-recapture assumptions are frequently tested: marks must not affect survival; the population must not change between catches (closed population).
Know and be able to apply the formula: population = (n1 × n2) ÷ m2, where n1 = first catch, n2 = second catch, m2 = number of marked individuals in second catch.
commonMistakes: Placing quadrats non-randomly (e.g. choosing nice patches or areas with lots of plants) — this introduces sampling bias and gives unrepresentative results.
Trying to use mark-release-recapture for plants — plants cannot be released back into a mixed population! Use quadrats for stationary organisms.
Forgetting the assumptions of mark-release-recapture — if animals die or migrate between captures, or if marks make animals more visible to predators, the estimate will be inaccurate.
clozePassages: Sampling is used to estimate the size of a population without counting every individual. A quadrat is a square frame placed randomly in a habitat. The number of organisms within it is counted and an average is calculated. The result is scaled up to estimate the total population. Quadrats are suitable for plants and slow-moving animals. Stratified sampling ensures samples are taken from all areas of a habitat proportionally.

The capture-recapture method is used to estimate the population size of mobile animals. A sample is captured, marked, and released. After sufficient time for mixing, a second sample is captured. The proportion of marked individuals in the second sample is used to calculate the population size using the formula: population size = (first capture × second capture) ÷ number of marked individuals recaptured. This assumes the marking does not affect survival.

A transect is a line placed across a habitat to study the distribution of organisms. At regular intervals along the transect, a quadrat is placed and species recorded. This is called a belt transect. Transects are useful for studying how communities change across an environmental gradient, such as from a seashore to inland or from the edge to the centre of a woodland. They reveal patterns of zonation in species distribution.
